summary: Updates the ASN.1 modules for Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and related S/MIME formats from the 1988 to the 2002 version of ASN.1. There are no changes to the bits on the wire, only to the description syntax. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5911 rewrites ASN.1 modules for CMS and related S/MIME formats using the 2002 version of ASN.1. The encoded messages stay the same; only the notation used to describe them changes.

questions: what is the difference between asn.1 1988 and 2002
does rfc 5911 change the cms wire format
subtitle: CMS and S/MIME use the 2002 ASN.1 notation without changing their encoded messages.

tldr.problem: CMS and related formats were described using the 1988 version of ASN.1, which had been deprecated. Developers wanted modules using the 2002 version.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC republishes ASN.1 modules from ten earlier RFCs in the 2002 syntax and adds a common AlgorithmInformation module. It replaces open-ended ANY fields with object classes and objects.
tldr.outcome: The change is to the descriptive syntax only; the wire formats do not change. RFC 5911 is Informational and was updated by RFC 6268.

today: RFC 5911 is an Informational document updated by RFC 6268. The RFC changes the ASN.1 notation but states that the wire formats do not change.

sections.title: Why the Modules Were Rewritten
sections.content:
CMS and associated formats use ASN.1 to describe their data structures. Many security-related RFCs still used ASN.1 from the 1988 standard, which had been deprecated. RFC 5911 updates a set of modules to conform to the 2002 version.

The set covers modules from ten RFCs related to CMS algorithms, AES in CMS, S/MIME, firmware protection, evidence records, and other CMS formats. Some modules are included to make the collection complete. The companion RFC 5912 contains related PKIX modules.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC updates the notation used to describe CMS and related formats. It includes modules from earlier RFCs and a shared module used by the collection.

sections.title: A Shared Algorithm Module
sections.content:
Section 2 defines AlgorithmInformation, a common ASN.1 module that did not come from an earlier RFC. Other modules use it to describe algorithm categories and their properties, including digest, signature, public-key, key-transport, key-agreement, key-wrap, key-derivation, MAC, and content-encryption algorithms.

The document's modules, combined with those in RFC 5912, are intended to stand on their own without importing definitions from elsewhere. Comments inside the modules still cite original RFCs, and some cited documents may have been superseded.
sections.plainLanguage: AlgorithmInformation defines shared descriptions used by many of the modules. This lets the updated modules refer to algorithm types consistently.

sections.title: Objects Replace Open-Ended Fields
sections.content:
The modules make extensive use of the object model in the 2002 ASN.1 documents. Where 1988 syntax used ANY fields to permit variable syntax, the new modules use objects instead.

The document also recommends prefixes that identify the kind of object. For example, id-sha1 names an object identifier, while mda-sha1 names a message-digest object. Object sets use consistent names and are qualified by their module names when imported.
sections.plainLanguage: The new notation replaces a general-purpose ANY field with named object types. Prefixes also make it easier to see what kind of object a name represents.

sections.title: The Wire Format Is Unchanged
sections.content:
The RFC states that no format has any bits-on-the-wire changes. The update changes the syntax used to describe the formats, not the encoded messages produced by implementations.

As a result, an implementation based on the new modules should encode and decode the same message bytes as one based on the earlier descriptions, assuming both implement the same formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the written description changes. CMS and S/MIME messages keep the same encoded bytes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that although the covered formats relate to security, this document itself has no security considerations. The ASN.1 modules retain the same bits-on-the-wire as the modules they replace.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC changes notation, not the encoded formats. It says the update itself introduces no security considerations.
